note.question: Which competitors voluntarily merge when one firm is large, two are capacity constrained, and each has captive customers—and should antitrust authorities approve the resulting structure?
note.overview: Three price-setting competitors endogenously choose whether and with whom to merge. For each feasible market structure the firms play explicit mixed-strategy pricing games, and a strong-Nash stability concept rules out profitable individual and coalition deviations across structures.

models.method: The authors derive price-support distributions and equilibrium profits for each feasible ownership structure, apply strong-Nash deviation inequalities to select endogenous mergers, compare competition intensity through support lower bounds, and evaluate social welfare and consumer surplus analytically and numerically.

sources.quote: In summary, when all three firms have the same size of loyal buyers, only the independent structure {A,B,C} and the mixed merger structure {AB,C} are possible to emerge as the equilibrium, and the small merger struc­ ture {A,BC} will never be sustainable.17 Will the small merger structure ever emerge as the equilibrium when firms have different loyal segment sizes?

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Starting from three independent firms, the stable market structure is selected by strong-Nash coalition-stability conditions rather than by an explicit proposal protocol: no individual firm or coalition can profitably replace it with another permitted two-firm merger or independence, allowing merger profit to be allocated among members. Conditional on a structure, the remaining entities simultaneously set prices, after which demand and capacity-constrained rationing mechanically determine sales and profits. Mergers pool both capacity and loyal buyers and reduce the number of price competitors. Capacity asymmetry softens price competition, while a larger merged loyal segment makes the merged entity less aggressive and can divert switchers to the outsider.
